title: Anticholinergic Burden, Arthritis and Frailty: A Safer Medicines Review
meta_title: Anticholinergic Burden and Arthritis: Medicines Review
meta_description: What anticholinergic burden means, which medicines to check, limits of scores and dementia evidence, and how to ask for a safe medicines review.
excerpt: Check the whole medicine list, not just a burden score. Practical review questions, evidence limits and the urgent route for sudden confusion.
direct_answer: Anticholinergic burden is the combined effect of medicines that block acetylcholine. Some pain, bladder, allergy and sleep medicines can add to it. Ask your pharmacist or prescriber to review benefits and side effects together. Do not stop prescribed treatment yourself. Sudden new confusion needs A&E or 999.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: anticholinergic burden, medicines review, older people, falls, confusion, arthritis, frailty, UK

content:
Quick answer: Anticholinergic burden is the combined effect of medicines that block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger. It can matter when arthritis pain medicines are taken alongside bladder, allergy or sleep medicines, especially in older people living with frailty. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber to review the whole list, not just a score. Do not stop prescribed treatment yourself. Sudden new confusion needs A&E or 999, not a routine medicines review.

What anticholinergic burden means

Some medicines block acetylcholine as part of their intended action; in others, that effect is unwanted. One strongly anticholinergic medicine, or several with smaller effects, can create a significant combined burden. It is sometimes called anticholinergic load.

This is not the same as the number of tablets you take. Taking several useful medicines is not automatically inappropriate. The question is whether each medicine still helps you, what unwanted effects it causes and how the combination fits your health and priorities. NICE medicines optimisation guidance describes a medication review as an agreed examination of treatment, its benefits, safety and problems.

Why this matters when you have arthritis

An arthritis prescription is only part of the picture. You may also take something for nerve pain, bladder urgency, hay fever, travel sickness or sleep. A medicine bought without a prescription can add to the effects of prescribed treatment.

Possible problems include dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, difficulty passing urine and problems with thinking or memory. Dizziness or sleepiness can also make daily activities harder. If sore joints already make it difficult to get up, walk or reach the toilet, these effects are worth discussing rather than accepting as inevitable ageing.

Older people living with frailty may have less reserve when medicines cause problems. But a symptom does not prove anticholinergic burden is the cause: infection, dehydration, other medicines and medical conditions may need assessment too. Do not use this explanation to dismiss a sudden change as a routine side effect.

Which medicines are worth checking?

The examples below are reasons to ask for a review, not a list of medicines everyone should avoid or replace.

  • Amitriptyline for pain. The NHS pain-medicine page describes dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, sleepiness and difficulty peeing. Lower pain doses can still cause side effects. Its benefits and your actual symptoms matter, not simply the fact that it appears on a burden list.
  • Bladder medicines such as oxybutynin. These may be helping urgency or leakage, while also causing dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision or trouble emptying the bladder. The NHS oxybutynin guide gives medicine-specific advice. A replacement is not automatically suitable for you.
  • Some sedating antihistamines and sleep aids. Diphenhydramine is sold in some sleep products. NHS guidance notes sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness and concentration problems, with side effects more likely over 65. Check active ingredients, including combination cold or night-time products.
  • Some sickness medicines and other specialist treatment. Scottish prescribing guidance lists several medicine groups and stresses that alternatives can have other risks. Changes to specialist medicines may need specialist advice.

This is not a complete interaction check. Bring the exact product names, strengths and how you actually use them. Do not assume every arthritis medicine is anticholinergic, or that a medicine with little anticholinergic effect is free of other risks.

What can a burden score tell you?

A pharmacist may use an Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden scale or another tool to flag combinations worth reviewing. NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service describes tools that help professionals assess anticholinergic effects alongside other medicine risks.

A score is a prompt for clinical judgement, not a diagnosis, a personal prediction of dementia or an instruction to stop tablets. NICE dementia guidance, recommendations 1.6.1 to 1.6.3, recognises medicines associated with cognitive impairment and advises considering lower-burden options during relevant assessments and reviews. It says there is insufficient evidence to recommend one burden tool over the others.

Scottish guidance also notes disagreements between sources and that parts of scoring tables rely on incomplete evidence or expert opinion. The prescriber still needs to consider the medicine's purpose, dose, your symptoms, other illnesses and what an alternative might do. Do not chase a particular online number as a treatment target.

Does reducing the burden prevent dementia?

That has not been established. Studies linking anticholinergic exposure with cognitive problems are a reason to review prescribing carefully, but an association does not show what caused one person's memory changes.

A Cochrane review published in 2023 found three small trials involving 299 older adults. Follow-up was only one to three months and the evidence was very uncertain. The review could not establish whether reducing anticholinergic medicines safely preserves or improves cognition; the trials did not investigate safety outcomes. This does not mean reviews are pointless, or that stopping a useful medicine is proven to prevent dementia.

If memory has gradually worsened, arrange a GP assessment. If confusion starts suddenly, use the emergency advice below instead of waiting for a memory appointment.

Prepare for a useful medicines review

Ask your GP practice or pharmacist how to arrange a review of the whole medicine list. You can say: "I am worried about dry mouth, constipation or unsteadiness. Could we check anticholinergic burden and other medicine effects together?" A review is not a commitment to stop treatment.

  1. Bring the real list. Include prescribed medicines, pharmacy products, supplements, inhalers, drops, creams and anything taken only occasionally. Packets or photographs can help identify active ingredients. Mention recent hospital changes and medicines you are no longer taking.
  2. Describe the change. Note when symptoms began, whether a medicine was started or its dose changed, falls or near-falls, bowel or bladder problems and effects on daily activities. A timeline helps the clinician; it does not prove the cause.
  3. Explain what treatment gives you. Better sleep, less nerve pain or fewer urgent toilet trips may matter greatly. Ask how those benefits could be retained if treatment changes.
  4. Agree the next step. Options may include continuing with monitoring, changing timing or dose, a different medicine or a supervised gradual reduction. Ask what to watch for, who to contact and when the plan will be reviewed.

SPS guidance on person-centred reviews stresses agreed goals, risks and benefits, communication and follow-up. If you want, involve someone who helps with your medicines. Ask for a written plan that you and the people supporting you can understand.

Do not make a stopping plan from this article

Do not stop or reduce a prescribed medicine because an online calculator gives it a high score. Some medicines need gradual withdrawal or specialist input. For example, the NHS advises against suddenly stopping amitriptyline without talking to your doctor. A clinician may recommend a gradual reduction over weeks or longer, depending on the person. This article does not provide a taper schedule.

Follow the leaflet's medicine-specific instructions for suspected serious side effects and get help promptly. Do not drive or use machinery if a medicine makes you dizzy, drowsy or unable to see clearly. A routine review must not delay urgent assessment.

When to get medical help

  • Go to A&E or call 999 if someone suddenly becomes confused. NHS sudden-confusion guidance treats this as needing immediate assessment. Do not assume it is dementia or a medicine effect. Do not drive yourself. Stay with the person, reassure them and bring their medicine list if you can.
  • Call 999 for a seizure, someone who cannot be woken, severe breathing difficulty or signs of a serious allergic reaction. Do not wait for a medicines-review appointment.
  • Speak to a doctor urgently if you cannot pee at all. NHS amitriptyline and oxybutynin guidance gives this advice. For difficulty starting or emptying your bladder, contact your doctor or NHS 111 promptly. Do not wait for a routine review.
  • Arrange a GP appointment for gradually worsening memory or persistent troublesome side effects. Bring details of the symptoms and all medicines. Sudden confusion follows the emergency route above.

Common questions

Does taking amitriptyline mean it is unsafe for me?

No. Its suitability depends on its benefits, dose, other treatment and your health. Discuss symptoms and concerns with the prescriber. Do not stop it suddenly yourself.

Can a pharmacy sleep aid count if I only take it sometimes?

Yes. Include occasional products in the review and tell the pharmacist what else you take. Check the active ingredient rather than relying on the brand name or assuming non-prescription means harmless.

Will a lower score fix falls or memory problems?

It is not a guarantee. These problems can have several causes, and the evidence does not establish that reducing the score prevents dementia. A personalised review should consider symptoms, treatment benefits, alternatives and follow-up.
